interest: This file provides valuable insight into the granular economic and agricultural monitoring conducted by the Allied Occupation authorities in postwar Japan. It illustrates how the U.S. Department of Agriculture and SCAP tracked minor cash crops and garden produce—such as red peppers and staple tubers (white potatoes and sweet potatoes)—to assess Japan's potential for export earnings, food self-sufficiency, and commercial reintegration into the American market. The records also illuminate the multi-tiered administrative chain of communication connecting U.S. civilian departments (Agriculture and State), military occupation headquarters (SCAP and the Department of the Army), and the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture, demonstrating how statistical intelligence was collected, priced, and transmitted across agencies.
overview: This file (894.614 Agriculture., Japan, Garden Crops., February 24, 1948 – July 29, 1949) consists of diplomatic correspondence—four telegrams and one airgram—exchanged between the U.S. Department of State in Washington and the Office of the United States Political Advisor (USPOLAD) in Tokyo, liaising with the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP). The records document efforts by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to obtain production statistics, export availability, and pricing data for Japanese garden crops during the Allied Occupation. Early 1948 messages focus specifically on red pepper production, detailing yield estimates and maximum export prices for commercial varieties such as Yatsufusa and Hontonka. A July 1949 airgram outlines the reporting schedule and communication channels through SCAP's Natural Resources Section and the Department of the Army for forthcoming 1949 Japanese white potato and sweet potato crop estimates.

subfiles.about: The Department of State requests telegraphic estimates from USPOLAD Tokyo on Japan's current production, export availability, and market price of red pepper.
subfiles.from: George C. Marshall (Secretary of State, on behalf of the Department of Agriculture)
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State George C. Marshall transmits an urgent inquiry from the Department of Agriculture to the U.S. Political Advisor in Tokyo. The message requests telegraphic estimates of current Japanese red pepper production, the quantity expected to become available for export, and prevailing market prices. It marks the opening inquiry in the file concerning Japanese specialty garden crop exports during the occupation.
subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram from Marshall to USPOLAD Tokyo requesting Japanese red pepper production and export estimates

subfiles.about: The Department of State asks for a detailed breakdown of 1948 Japanese red pepper production by variety, FOB prices, and projected exports to the United States.
subfiles.from: George C. Marshall (Secretary of State, on behalf of the Department of Agriculture)
subfiles.summary: Following up on Tokyo's preliminary telegram of March 1, Secretary of State Marshall requests further detailed data on Japanese red peppers for the Department of Agriculture. The telegram requests a breakdown of the estimated 1,800 metric tons of 1948 production by specific variety, particularly Yatsufusa and Hontonka. It also seeks f.o.b. prices in U.S. cents per pound for each variety and projected 1948 export volumes destined for the United States.
subfiles.title: Outgoing telegram from Marshall to SCAP and USPOLAD Tokyo requesting red pepper variety breakdown and prices
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) and United States Political Advisor, Tokyo

subfiles.about: USPOLAD Tokyo reports preliminary 1947 production, 1948 projected yields, export availability, and f.o.b. prices for Japanese red peppers.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald (United States Political Advisor, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Replying to Department telegram 60, William J. Sebald reports that Japan produced approximately 600 metric tons of red peppers in 1947. Production for 1948 is estimated to increase to 1,800 metric tons, roughly two-thirds of which is expected to be available for export. The current f.o.b. Japan price is cited as approximately 17 U.S. cents per pound.
subfiles.title: Incoming telegram from Sebald to Secretary of State reporting Japanese red pepper production and export prices

subfiles.about: USPOLAD Tokyo transmits Japanese Ministry of Agriculture estimates on red pepper yields, export quotas, and maximum prices for the Hontonka and Yatsufusa varieties.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald (United States Political Advisor, Tokyo)
subfiles.summary: Responding to Department telegram 134, Sebald provides detailed data from the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture regarding the 1948 red pepper crop. Hontonka production is estimated at 800,000 pounds with 50% available for export at an f.o.b. price of roughly 17 cents per pound, while Yatsufusa production is estimated at 2,200,000 pounds with 50% exportable at 14 cents per pound. These prices represent ceiling maximums subject to reduction, and an additional 440 metric tons of miscellaneous red pepper varieties are noted without specific price or type breakdowns.
subfiles.title: Incoming telegram from Sebald to Secretary of State on red pepper varieties, production, and maximum export prices

subfiles.about: USPOLAD Tokyo relays SCAP's schedule for transmitting Japanese Government production estimates for the 1949 white potato and sweet potato crops.
subfiles.summary: In response to an inquiry from the Office of Foreign Agricultural Relations transmitted in June 1949, Sebald communicates information received from SCAP's Natural Resources Section. Production data on Japan's 1949 white potato crop will be forwarded to the Department of the Army via radio before October 1 for delivery to the Department of Agriculture. Sweet potato estimates will not be released by the Japanese Government until October 10, after which they will be forwarded immediately to Washington.
subfiles.title: Incoming airgram from USPOLAD Tokyo on transmission schedule for 1949 potato and sweet potato production estimates
